Website

Design direction

Fifteen photographs came in. Six go on the site. This is which six, where each one lives, and the one thing that has to happen before any of them can be published.

Read the permissions section before anything else. Every photograph in the set identifies a client, two carry another photographer's credit, and one shows a recognisable public figure. None of that is a problem. None of it is optional either.

Who we work with

Agencies, in-house teams & events professionals

We don't just work directly for event organisers. A large arm of our business is in supporting existing AV Teams & event agencies.

When a show starts to grow beyond your team's experience base, or when a technical requirement leaves you scratching your head, that's the time to call us!

Six departments

Take what you need

No photographs here, on purpose. Six small pictures of six dark rooms all look like the same show, and they would eat the entire library to say less than the words already do.

Set & Staging

In-house workshop and drawing. Large format prints from 30cm to 30m. Stock panels that get reused.

Lighting

LED fixtures throughout. Rigging worked out alongside the set, the screens and the PA rather than after them.

Sound

Calculated audio, not fly and hope. d&b PA, digital radio mics, digital desks.

Video

Colour space, resolution, viewing distance. Fibre transmission. Redundancy as standard.

Power

Designed with fuel in mind. Generators, distros, RCBOs throughout, logging where it's needed.

Content

Made to suit the screens, by the people running them. Upload portal, slide fixing, speaker preview.

The people on your show

We get it. You want the person you know.

Not a project manager assigned the week before. Not the new starter playing catchup.

You want the person who quoted it, the person who flagged that pinch point, the person who said it would work if you do that one specific thing. You want them in the room, on the build.

02 · The room Permission needed The best photograph in the set. Empty, symmetrical, properly shot, and the wide LED and star cloth show the build rather than the event. This is the one that makes the site look like it belongs to a company that works at this scale.
Note what black is doing. The photographs run red, magenta, purple, teal and blue, and no two share a palette. Black is the only ground that lets them sit on one page without fighting, which is also why the cyan accent never goes near a picture. On white, or on any tinted section, this set would look like a jumble.
Allocation

Six photographs, and where each one goes

With six, the decision that matters is not which pictures to take but which ones to leave out. Two rules hold the whole thing together: no image appears small, and no page carries two. Break either and six starts to look like a shortage.

Why the departments get none

Six small photographs of six dark rooms all look like the same show. They would consume the entire library to say less than the words already say, and they would put every image below the size where it does any work.

The grid is stronger typographic anyway. A producer reading it is scanning for whether we cover their gap, and a list answers that faster than a picture does.

What the set is missing

All fifteen are finished rooms. There is no workshop, no build in progress, no crew, no get-in, nothing back of house, and no daylight except the two outdoor set shots.

So the site can prove we deliver events and cannot yet prove there's a company behind them. That's the gap worth one hour to close, and it's the one the copy leans on hardest.

Deliberately not chosen, and they were close. Two more empty stages with printed sets, a huge blue LED wall with beams through haze, a magenta uplit set, a panel discussion, an exhibition floor. All good. All variations on rooms already covered. The six above were picked for range rather than quality: audience, empty build, awards, cabaret, foyer, fabrication. Six near-identical stages would make a smaller-looking company than six different rooms.
Why photo-led

Photographs are the proof we can publish without asking permission

The urgent job is verify. Someone has our name and searches it. Copy can be written by anyone in an afternoon; a photograph of a real build, in a real venue, with real crew in it, cannot be faked or borrowed. It does that job in under a second, before anyone reads a sentence.

That matters more here than most places, because the two things that would normally do this work aren't available to us. Testimonials are awkward when the work is white-label, since asking an agency to praise its subcontractor asks them to admit they used one. Named case studies need written permission per client, which is still outstanding.

There's a second reason, and it's about register. The voice is deliberately quiet. Quiet copy on a plain page reads as thin. Quiet copy with strong photography reads as confident, because the pictures carry the scale so the words don't have to. It's the combination that lets us stop making claims.

Which is why the one rule that cannot bend is no stock. Every competitor uses it and everyone in this industry recognises it on sight. It says either that we have no work of our own to show, or that we think the reader won't notice. Both are worse than an empty page.

Permissions

All fifteen identify a client. None can go up yet.

This is the finding that matters, and it isn't a criticism of the set. The photographs are good. But the clearance model in the earlier draft assumed a stock of unattributable material to launch on, and there isn't any.

Every one

Client permission

Logos on set, branded LED, sponsor walls, printed step-and-repeat. In every single frame a reader could name whose event it was, which under the naming rule is the same as writing the name in text.

It's usually a yes and it's a two-line email. But it's fifteen conversations, or six if we only clear what we're using, and it has to happen before Will builds the pages.

Two of them

Photographer's licence

Two images carry another photographer's credit in the corner. Being the production company on the job doesn't give us the right to publish their photograph.

Separate permission, separate person, and usually granted for a credit line. Worth asking, because they're among the best in the set. Don't crop the credit out.

One of them

A recognisable individual

One shows a panel including a public figure whose presence at that event is itself newsworthy.

Different question again, and the honest answer is that we don't need it. The image says nothing about our work that the other fourteen don't. Leave it out and the problem goes away.

The clean-twin habit still matters, and it's now the priority. Every one of these was shot after the branding went up. The same rooms, photographed an hour earlier or from three feet to the side, would have been publishable the day they were taken with nobody's permission needed. That habit is worth more than any single photograph on this list.

What to actually do

Clear the six, not the fifteen. One email per client, naming the event and attaching the frame. Ask for the website and social, not "marketing use", because the narrower ask gets the faster yes.

If one comes back no, there are nine reserves and the layout doesn't change.

Why not just anonymise them

Blurring a logo on a set that a producer would recognise anyway looks worse than asking. This industry is small, people know whose show that was, and a blurred client reads as a supplier who didn't ask.

The permission is the cheaper option and it's also the one that strengthens the relationship rather than risking it.

How photographs are used

Four rules, and the reasons

Do

  • Full bleed, edge to edge. No gutter, no rounded corners, no shadow, no border. It reads as confident and it makes a small library look bigger, because each image gets more room
  • Black as the ground. The logo is a black circle and the work happens in dark rooms. Dark sections let the photographs be the light source: they glow, the page recedes
  • Text next to pictures, or on the flat black between them. The one exception is the hero, where the image is chosen for the space rather than the space forced onto the image
  • Cyan as a signal. Eyebrows, rules, one word in a headline, links. It appears rarely enough to mean something

Don't

  • Headlines over busy images. This is where most supplier sites fall apart, and the usual fix is a black gradient over the whole picture, which ruins the photograph to save the text
  • A white page with photo cards. Every image becomes a bright rectangle in a bright field, and the whole thing reads as a brochure about venues rather than the inside of one
  • Cyan as a background field, or as a tint over a photograph. A lot of what we shoot already has cool blue-white light in it, so the accent belongs to the pictures rather than being applied on top
  • Middle type sizes. Big headings and normal body, nothing in between. Middle sizes are what make a page look like a template
Palette

Cyan, not green

Sampled from the round logo. Everything written in this repo before 27 August called it green, on my assumption that the signage was photographing cyan under its LEDs. It wasn't. The signage was accurate.

Brand#008EAA
Accent, light#007A93
Accent, dark#00C2E8
Ground#000000
Raised, dark#12191C
Raised, light#F4F8F9
Why the accent isn't the brand value. #008EAA on white is 3.85:1, which fails accessibility for body text. #007A93 is 4.99:1 and reads as the same colour. True value on fills, rules and display type where the ratio doesn't apply; accent for anything at reading size.

The gap

Fifteen finished rooms, and nothing else

Every photograph is the same moment in the job: the room, finished, before or during the event. There is nothing from the other ninety per cent of the work.

No workshop. No build. No crew. No get-in. No cable, no distro, no truss going up, nobody on a ladder.

That matters because it's precisely what the copy claims. The home page argues that what you're buying is the people and the way they're picked. The Set & Staging page talks about an in-house workshop, CNC, stock panels that get reused. None of it has a picture, and the one argument the site makes hardest is the one with no evidence behind it.

Two hours fixes it, and needs nobody's permission

One hour in the workshop. Wide with the lights on, benches as they are, a print coming off, panels stacked, the CNC mid-cut. Don't tidy it: a tidied workshop looks like a showroom, a working one looks like a company.

Ten minutes mid-build on the next show. Crew working, mid-distance, backs to camera, nobody posed. Truss going up, deck going down.

Both are Tier 1. No logos, no clients, nothing to clear. They can go up the day they're taken, and between them they'd close the only real hole in the set.

And the free one, still the best idea here. The same room from one fixed spot, three times across a day: empty, mid-build, finished. Thirty seconds each, from a position someone is standing in anyway. Nobody in this industry publishes it, and it would explain the whole business without a word of copy.
The way this fails

The blocker moved, and it moved somewhere better

Until this morning the risk was that no photographs existed. They do, and they're better than the plan assumed. The risk now is fifteen emails that nobody sends, which is the same shape as the problem that held the copy up for eight months.

It's smaller than it looks. Six emails, one per client, each two lines with the frame attached. Half an hour of someone's afternoon, and most will answer the same day. If one says no, there are nine reserves and the layout doesn't move.

Build the slots so swapping a photograph is an upload, not a layout change, and the site can launch on four while the last two come back.

⛔ Four things before this is finished.

1. Six permission emails, one per client, plus one to the photographer whose credit is on two of the frames. Nothing else on this list blocks the build.

2. Two hours with a camera: an hour in the workshop, ten minutes mid-build on the next show. Tier 1, nobody's permission needed, and it closes the only real hole in the set.

3. The logo as SVG. Still in SharePoint, which this session can't reach. The 256px PNG is fine for a favicon and not for a site header.

4. Six numbers per show for the three case studies: people in the room, rooms or spaces, get-in hours, crew on site, days on site, and roughly who it was for. The pictures are here, the numbers next to them aren't.
